SOURCE DETAIL FOR SELF-STUDY
PART 1 · CORE CONCEPTS
11
CONCEPT 4 · THE ESCALATION LADDER
Prompt it → feed it documents → retrain it
1 · PROMPT IT
instructions to a skilled temp
Fixes BEHAVIOR — tone, format, focus, approach.
Free · instant · every model. 90% of the value — this course.
2 · FEED IT DOCUMENTS
hand the temp your binder (RAG)
Fixes MISSING KNOWLEDGE — your policies, your data, current facts.
Minutes to set up · citable · private. Most real cases end here.
3 · RETRAIN IT
send it back to school (fine-tuning)
Changes deep HABITS — permanently.
Slow · expensive · per-model. Rare: an IT project, not a prompt.
One topic, up the ladder — “answer customer questions about our warranty policy”
①  “Answer in plain language and quote the exact clause.” Answers get clear and consistent — but it doesn’t KNOW our policy, so the details are guesses.
②  Upload the warranty documents (or use the company assistant). Now: current, cited answers from the real text. This is where you stop.
③  Retrain — only if millions of chats must carry a deep habit with no room for instructions. An IT decision, not a prompt.
One question picks the rung: is the AI missing knowledge → feed it documents. Misbehaving with knowledge it has → prompt it. Retraining stays rare.

ARCHIVED SOURCE NOTES
HOW TO PRESENT —
1) The three big cards LEFT TO RIGHT — say the verbs: prompt it, feed it documents, retrain it. The temp analogies carry it: instructions → binder → back to school.
2) Then the worked topic, ① → ② → ③, warranty questions: prompting fixes the HOW, documents fix the WHAT, and step ② is where almost every real workplace case ends. Step ③ exists so the room knows what it is — and that it isn’t their job.
3) Amber band — the takeaway question, verbatim: missing knowledge → documents; misbehaving → prompt.

BRIDGE —
“Two concepts left — the next one is all about the bill.”

ACRONYMS —
RAG = Retrieval-Augmented Generation (rung 2 — the open-book exam from the previous slide).

CONTENT —
v1.7: rebuilt as three big sequential steps + one worked topic (owner request); the guided-prompt chip and on-slide drill were cut — the six-problem triage drill survives in workbook tab BONUS-Ladder for self-study (answers: 1 P · 2 R · 3 P · 4 R · 5 F · 6 defensible either way).
“Let’s fine-tune on our procedures” → first ask: knowledge problem (→documents) or behavior problem (→prompt)? Most enterprise cases are knowledge problems.
Frontier flagships mostly aren’t fine-tunable (2026); open-weight models are.
NOTE: this is the ESCALATION ladder (capability). Part 6’s PROMOTION ladder (where prompts live) is a different ladder — name them fully.

SOURCE DETAIL FOR SELF-STUDY
PART 1 · CORE CONCEPTS
12
CONCEPT 5 · FAST MODELS VS THINKING MODELS
Two speeds, one bill
Every vendor ships a fast tier — one pass, instant, cheap — and a thinking tier that drafts, checks and revises internally before answering.
System 1 vs System 2 (Kahneman’s Thinking, Fast and Slow): fast intuition for routine asks; slow deliberation where being wrong is expensive.
The bill: thinking is charged as output tokens — the expensive kind. A hard question can quietly cost 5–20× a simple one.
Why the fast tier got so good: MoE (Part 2 tells that story) and big models teaching small ones (distillation).
Think ON: multi-step analysis · math · root-cause work · code · tradeoffs across a long document.
Think OFF: lookups · reformatting · summaries · routine drafting — deliberation you don’t need.
PROMPT 5/7
Same brain, two speeds
TYPE THIS → “Describe your fast mode vs your thinking mode like I’m choosing between them for real work: when is each worth it, and roughly how much more does thinking cost? Under 120 words.”
WHY → the model explains its own two speeds — and its own bill.
✂ copy-paste, don’t retype: tab EX5-TwoSpeeds of your Course Workbook
The two speeds, side by side
FAST — one pass, instant, cheap. Great until the question has traps.
THINKING — drafts, checks, revises. 5–20× the cost.

ARCHIVED SOURCE NOTES
HOW TO PRESENT —
1) Frame: “every AI app sells you two speeds — when is the slow one worth its bill?” Name the book once: Kahneman’s Thinking, Fast and Slow — the owner-favorite narrative of this slide.
2) The BILL bullet is the slow-down: thinking is billed like output — 5–20× a simple ask.
3) Green/amber cards: on for, off for. Escalate on failure, not by default.

TRY IT — PROMPT 5/7 (copy from tab EX5-TwoSpeeds)
One send, informative. The extended puzzle version lives in the same tab for stretch time or homework.
Recovery (a model claims one mode): “ask it what the thinking toggle in its own interface does, then — that’s tomorrow’s exercise anyway.”

BRIDGE —
“That’s the two speeds. Now the whole menu — where your tokens actually go.”

ACRONYMS —
MoE = Mixture of Experts — defined properly in Part 2.
System 1 / System 2 = Kahneman’s fast-intuition vs slow-deliberation framing.

CONTENT —
v1.7: the on-slide extended-puzzle card was cut (owner: too much); the puzzle survives in the workbook tab’s EXTENDED rows for self-study (answer key: Ben Mon · Chloe Tue · Ema Wed · Ana Thu · Dev Fri).
Thinking tokens billed as output even when you only see a summary; output ≈ 5× input across vendors; effort adaptive/dial-able by 2026 (t4 §5, primary-sourced).
Honest caveat: the model isn’t literally “thinking” — it generates intermediate tokens that improve the final answer.
ART — the sprinting-hare / studying-tortoise panel is an owner-generated illustration (R16): hare = fast tier, tortoise = thinking tier. Name the fable, point at the panel.

title: Verification belongs in the task
notes:
MODE: TEACH

TIME: 0:50

PURPOSE: Build a concept required for the next application.

LAND THIS: Fluent answers can be wrong, so verification belongs in the work design.

SAY:
- Distinguish plausible language from evidence.
- Asking the same model “Are you sure?” is not independent verification.
- Name the source or calculation that would settle the question.

DO: None.

BRIDGE: Move to “Failure patterns and the check they need”.

IF LATE: COMPRESS

SOURCE DETAIL FOR SELF-STUDY
PART 1 · CORE CONCEPTS
14
CONCEPT 6 · HALLUCINATION
Fluency is not evidence
The mechanism: models are optimized for the most plausible next token, not the most true one. Trouble concentrates where training data is thin: rare facts, citations, numbers, names.
OpenAI’s own 2025 research: benchmarks reward confident guessing over “I don’t know” — models learn to be good test-takers.
The better word is confabulation: it fills gaps with plausible material, in-format — fake citations LOOK like citations.
The confident guess, measured
Older reasoning model (o4-mini)
24%
75%
Newer, trained to say “I don’t know”
22%
26%
52%
■ right  ■ wrong  ■ “I don’t know” — ~3× fewer false claims.
OpenAI’s own models & benchmark (2025) — the mechanism, not a vendor ranking.
THE CONFIDENT GUESS  · Invented facts
Free recall where data was thin — a wrong fact, delivered with total certainty.
THE FAKE RECEIPT  · Invented sources
Citations, cases, book titles that look perfectly real — and don’t exist.
THE JOKE TAKEN SERIOUSLY  · Wrong source, confident answer
Fluent, cited — and built on a joke, a satire, or the wrong revision.
GARBAGE IN, GOSPEL OUT  · Runs with your false premise
It assumes your prompt is true: feed it a wrong “fact” and it politely builds on it.

ARCHIVED SOURCE NOTES
HOW TO PRESENT —
1) Open with the improv actor, spoken: “an improv actor never breaks character — the show must go on, so gaps get filled with the most plausible line. That is your AI on a thin-data day.”
2) Left bullets: the mechanism; the bold OpenAI 2025 finding — the vendor itself says benchmarks reward guessing; the vocabulary upgrade — CONFABULATION.
3) Right: meet the four CHARACTERS — say the nicknames with theater: the confident guess · the fake receipt · the joke taken seriously · garbage in, gospel out. One line each; each returns as a real incident on the next slide.
4) The chart, bottom-left — read it in one breath: “same questions, two models, nearly the same amount RIGHT — but the older one GUESSED whenever it didn’t know (75% wrong), and the newer one was allowed to say I-don’t-know (wrong drops to 26%).” That is the confident guess, measured — and it is why Part 3 teaches you to give the model an out.
5) Presenter story for character 1 if you want one: Google Bard’s launch demo flubbed a telescope fact — details on the next slide’s notes.

BRIDGE —
“What do these characters look like in public? The hall of shame.”

ACRONYMS —
none new on this slide.

CONTENT —
v1.7: abstain-vs-guess chart added (r23: SimpleQA numbers from arXiv:2509.04664 + the GPT-5 system card — o4-mini 24/75/1 vs gpt-5-thinking-mini 22/26/52; the on-slide caveat is mandatory).
v1.8 ART — the four character cards now carry the owner-generated object emblems (R16): blank cue card in a spotlight · sealed receipt dissolving into pixels · rubber chicken on a specimen tray · crumpled paper in a gilded frame. Point at each emblem as you name its character.

title: Failure patterns and the check they need
notes:
MODE: REFERENCE

TIME: 0:10

PURPOSE: Preserve depth for self-study without consuming live practice time.

LAND THIS: A memorable failure matters only when it changes how participants check answers.

SAY:
- The useful lesson in a public failure is the missing check.
- Read the linked source before repeating a specific incident or numerical claim.

DO: None.

BRIDGE: Move to “Part 2: models and tools”.

IF LATE: SKIP

SOURCE DETAIL FOR SELF-STUDY
PART 1 · CORE CONCEPTS
15
CONCEPT 6 · THE HALL OF SHAME · CONTINUED
Real, public, verified — and all avoidable
Glue on pizza · May 2024
Google’s AI search told users to put glue in pizza sauce and eat a rock a day — it had read a joke forum comment and satire as advice. Global mockery; scaled back within days.
The ChatGPT lawyer · Jun 2023
A New York lawyer filed six cases that didn’t exist — then asked ChatGPT if they were real. It said yes. $5,000 sanction, apology letters ordered (Mata v. Avianca).
Air Canada’s chatbot · Feb 2024
The website bot invented a bereavement refund policy. A tribunal made the airline honor it — rejecting “the bot is a separate legal entity.” Your company owns what its chatbot says.
The Big Four arc · 2025–26
Deloitte partially refunded a government report over invented citations; EY pulled one where 16 of 27 references failed; KPMG’s agentic-AI-excellence report: 5 of 45 citations checked out.
Not one-offs: a legal tracker counted ~1,500 court decisions worldwide involving AI-fabricated citations by mid-2026.
The cure hasn’t changed: Ground it (give it the source) · Cite it (demand receipts + an “I don’t know” escape hatch) · Verify it (check what matters before it ships).
House rule: every uncited standard clause, date, number, or quote is a draft until verified.

ARCHIVED SOURCE NOTES
HOW TO PRESENT —
1) Walk the four cards — laugh at glue-on-pizza, then take the temperature down.
2) Glue on pizza, plainly: someone posted a JOKE; the AI served it as advice — “the joke taken seriously.”
3) The lawyer: he checked the fabrication WITH the fabricator. Verification lives OUTSIDE the tool.
4) Air Canada: small money (~CA$800), giant precedent.
5) The Big Four arc: three global consultancies, three fabricated-source scandals in nine months — the last one a report ABOUT doing AI well.
6) Amber → teal → red bands, in order; the house rule VERBATIM — policy, not advice.

BRIDGE —
“That closes the concepts — now, the tool landscape.”

ACRONYMS —
none new on this slide.

CONTENT —
All incidents verified with sources, dates and MANDATORY phrasing caveats in notes/research/r14_hallucination_incidents.md.
Reserve incidents for questions (r14): Bard’s launch flub (phrase carefully: shares fell ~8% — about $100B — after Reuters flagged the error AND a weak launch event) · Sun-Times fake reading list · the invented Turley scandal · mayor Hood (THREATENED suit; never filed) · Cohen (NOT sanctioned) · NYC MyCity chatbot · Whisper in hospitals (AP).
None of the cures eliminates hallucination — they convert unverifiable claims into verifiable ones.

Pick by task, not habit — September 2026

OpenAI · GPT-5.6 (Sol / Terra / Luna)

Anthropic · Fable/Opus/Sonnet 5 + Haiku
Best-in-class coding & agentic work

ARCHIVED SOURCE NOTES
[REFRESH QUARTERLY — owner: Oscar]

HOW TO PRESENT —
1) Frame: “six trading cards — the big bold line on each is what that assistant is genuinely KNOWN FOR. Pick by task, not habit.”

3) On Grok, the plain version: “Unhinged” is not a nickname — it is an actual personality setting in its voice app, by that name; and in July 2025 a bad update had it praising Hitler for sixteen hours before an apology. That is the trade-off of a deliberately less-filtered assistant.
4) On Copilot, land the licensing fact: Microsoft’s Cowork agent runs on Claude technology — tiers matter more than brand wars.
5) Footer: the trust question is TWO SLIDES AHEAD; fortes verified Sep 9, 2026 and they WILL move.

“One force reshaped this list — the Chinese open-weight wave.”

SWE-bench = Software Engineering benchmark — the standard test of coding-agent ability.
GDPval = OpenAI’s benchmark of 220 real knowledge-work tasks across 44 occupations.
CJR = Columbia Journalism Review (its Tow Center tested AI search citation accuracy).
X = the social platform (Grok’s data source).

TYPE THIS → “Explain Mixture of Experts like a colleague: a specialist hospital where only the relevant departments wake up per question — and why that made AI dramatically cheaper in 2025. Under 120 words.”
WHY → the MoE cheat-note lands in your course log.
✂ copy-paste, don’t retype: tab EX7-MoE of your Course Workbook

ARCHIVED SOURCE NOTES
HOW TO PRESENT —
1) Anchor the moment, LEFT top card: January 2025 — an open model rivals o1; Nvidia’s $589B day; and keep the cost claim honest — the famous $5.6M is the fuel bill for the final winning race, not the cost of the racing team (total hardware spend was estimated well over $500M).
2) LEFT teal card — POINT AT THE HOSPITAL IMAGE: the whole building is 671 billion parameters; the three lit windows are the ~37 billion that wake up for your question. You pay for the specialists consulted, not the whole building. Distillation = big models teaching small ones.
3) RIGHT top — the star of the slide: $60 against $2.19, and the bars are TRUE proportion (the R1 bar really is 27× shorter). A $100 o1 workload for $3.60.
4) RIGHT bottom: three benchmark pairs — matched on math and coding, behind on PhD science (be honest: not a clean sweep).
5) Close the loop to Part 1: THIS is why thinking modes and deep research became affordable for everyone.

TRY IT — PROMPT 7/7 (copy from tab EX7-MoE)
Optional if time is tight; the answer doubles as their MoE cheat-note in the log.

BRIDGE —
“So whose servers is your data on? The trust map.”

ACRONYMS —
MoE = Mixture of Experts — only a fraction of the model computes per token (671B built, ~37B working).
MIT license = a permissive open-source license. R1 = DeepSeek’s open reasoning model; o1 = OpenAI’s.
AIME / GPQA / SWE-bench = math-olympiad, PhD-science and coding-agent benchmarks.

CONTENT —
v1.6: bill promoted to hero position with true-proportion bars + 27× badge; MoE hospital drawn (owner request); benchmark chart compressed to three rows — MATH-500 (97.3 vs 96.4) and Codeforces (96.3 vs 96.6 percentile) cut for space, quote if asked.
v1.8 ART — the drawn hospital is replaced by the owner-generated night-hospital illustration (R16): three windows lit, exactly the ~37B-of-671B story. Point at the lit windows.
Chart data verified against the R1 paper (arXiv:2501.12948) — see notes/research/r13_reputations_r1.md.
Pricing: R1 $0.55/$2.19 vs o1 $15/$60 per M tokens (Jan 2025) = 27.3–27.4×.
Since then (if asked): DeepSeek stayed the open-weight value leader but slipped off the leading edge — NIST’s CAISI evaluation (May 2026) put it ~8 months behind the frontier.
What the wave brought beyond DeepSeek (spoken if useful): open weights with permissive licenses to self-host (Qwen the most-downloaded family; famously self-hosted by Airbnb) · price pressure that pushed OpenAI to ship its first open-weight models since GPT-2 (gpt-oss, Aug 2025) · trillion-parameter open agentic models (Kimi).
US–China top-model gap: ~3% (Stanford AI Index 2026), down from 18–32 points in 2023.

notes:

TIME: 0:50

PURPOSE: Build a concept required for the next application.

SAY:
- Company data rules depend on the actual account, service, contract, and configuration.
- A vendor’s home country alone does not describe every customer’s storage arrangement.
- Resolve uncertain access before an upload, using the organization’s approved guidance.

DO: None.

Residency = choosing where it lives. 
An enterprise feature: the same vendor can host your company tenant in the EU while its consumer app stores chats in the US.
The one question that settles it: 
ask IT which region and tier YOUR account runs on — your organization’s AI policy has the answer for everything else.

ARCHIVED SOURCE NOTES
[REFRESH QUARTERLY — owner: Oscar]

HOW TO PRESENT —
1) Frame: “one geography question — whose servers, in which country — and one account question. That’s the whole trust topic at our level.”
2) Walk the three region panels LEFT TO RIGHT. US: where the consumer apps live by default. EUROPE: the residency panel — these are BUSINESS-TIER features; slow on Microsoft (EU Data Boundary — but the Claude models inside Copilot sit OUTSIDE it; your IT team cares). CHINA & ASIA: read DeepSeek’s line verbatim — its own privacy policy says data is “stored in the People’s Republic of China”; Italy blocked the app over it (Jan 2025, not lifted).
3) The italic map line: SAME LOGO, DIFFERENT HOMES — the account tier decides which one yours is. That is the entire lesson.
4) Teal card: residency, defined once.
5) Amber card: the handoff — which region and tier YOUR account runs on is an IT question; the org’s AI policy answers everything else. (Deliberately NOT on this slide: any what-data-goes-where guidance — that is company policy’s territory, not this training’s.)
6) The restaurant-vs-cookbook aside if China comes up: using the app is eating at their restaurant (they see your order); downloaded open-weight MODELS are a cookbook IT can cook from at home — the app, not the model, is the risk.

BRIDGE —
“That’s the landscape. Part 3 — the craft itself.”

ACRONYMS —
PRC = People’s Republic of China. EU Data Boundary = Microsoft’s commitment to process EU data inside the EU.
AWS = Amazon Web Services. Entity List = the US federal trade-restriction list — a procurement red flag.

CONTENT —
v1.12 (owner edits, ported): the centered “same logo, different homes — the ACCOUNT TIER decides” line was removed from the slide — say it aloud instead when sweeping the panels; it remains the slide’s one-line lesson.
v1.7: rebuilt as the server-geography map (owner: focus on where servers are; no data-type guidance — that belongs to company policy). Swap the schematic band for the owner’s generated world-map backdrop when it lands in notes/intake/ (R16).
Presenter background (kept OFF-slide by design, from r11, researched Sep 9 2026): the major Western vendors train on CONSUMER chats by default and none train on enterprise-tier data · the famous 2025 leaks were all personal-account: ~300K+ Grok chats indexed by Google; “deleted” ChatGPT chats preserved for court (enterprise excluded) · Google consumer: reviewed chats kept up to 3 yrs · Kimi PRC storage; Z.ai Singapore processing, Entity-List parent · EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711, Jun 2025): even enterprise Copilot had a zero-click exfiltration hole — patched.
Defaults drift (Anthropic flipped consumer training Aug 2025; Microsoft Oct 2024) — re-verify quarterly.
Standing rule, always said aloud: your organization’s AI policy and approved-tool list outrank everything on this slide.
